summary.summary: Cardiff's cover report to Governance and Audit Committee summarises the 2024/25 Treasury Management Annual Report ahead of its submission to full Council: investments stood at £10.9m at 31 March 2025, all deemed recoverable with no losses required to be recognised in the accounts, generating £2.6m of interest for the General Fund. External borrowing was £980m at 31 March 2025, after £100.9m of new borrowing and £14.7m of scheduled repayments during the year; interest payable was £37.5m, of which £16.1m was charged to the Housing Revenue Account. The council reports no breach of its prudential indicators requiring a separate report to Council during 2024/25.

signals.headline: No breach of 2024/25 prudential indicators reported to Council; all £10.9m of investments at 31 March 2025 deemed recoverable with no losses recognised.
signals.why: A verified-quiet compliance read for the year, though this cover report alone does not carry the full appendix's detailed maturity/indicator tables.

news_drafts.headline: Cardiff Council faces £167m budget gap over four years as savings plans fall short
news_drafts.lead: Cardiff Council is facing a projected budget shortfall of £167.1 million between 2027/28 and 2030/31, the Governance and Audit Committee heard on 24 September. The council balanced its 2025/26 budget but acknowledged that delivery of its savings programme is proving uneven: efficiency savings hit 88 per cent of target at £10.9 million, while service change proposals achieved only 76 per cent at £2.3 million. The Audit Committee noted that while the overall position was balanced, some directorates recorded significant overspends requiring control improvements. The council is also facing sustained demand pressures in social care, schools and education, particularly in support for additional learning needs. In a separate governance change, the former Section 151 Officer (chief finance officer) was promoted to Chief Executive in August, with the Deputy Section 151 Officer holding the role on an interim basis for up to 12 months while the senior management structure is reviewed. The council has been explicit about the risk that a Chief Executive permanently holding both roles would compromise independent financial challenge — guidance from the profession's standards body requires the Section 151 Officer to operate independently from the Chief Executive.

news_drafts.headline: Auditor finds no material uncertainty over Cardiff Harbour Authority continuing for 12 months
news_drafts.lead:
The external auditor (the independent check on the accounts) has concluded that Cardiff Harbour Authority's accounts can properly be prepared on a "going concern" basis, meaning the body is expected to keep operating. The conclusion is in an appendix to item 7.1 on the agenda of the Governance and Audit Committee, which met on 22 September 2026.

The auditor says it has "not identified any material uncertainties" about events or conditions that, singly or together, "may cast significant doubt" on the authority's ability to adopt that basis. The test covers at least twelve months from the date the financial statements are authorised for issue.

The paper is the auditor's own report on the going concern question, in its own words, rather than the council's description of itself. The papers put before the committee give no figures with it.

news_drafts.headline: Cardiff faces £164m budget gap with no plan yet to close half of it
news_drafts.lead: Cardiff Council faces a budget deficit of £163.7m over the next four years, with only £45m of savings identified against a required £119m, the council's Cabinet heard this week. The gap reflects cost pressures of £223.7m against funding increases of just £60m across 2027/28 to 2030/31. The council is assuming a 2% annual rise in Welsh Government grants, but has no formal guidance beyond 2026/27; a 1% shortfall in funding would create £7.2m of additional cuts. Schools face an aggregate deficit of £9.6m by March 2027 after reserves fell £27m in four years. The council holds reserves at the lower end of adequacy for an authority of its size, limiting its ability to absorb economic shocks. Scenario modelling shows the gap could range from £17m in optimistic conditions to £290m if funding remains flat and inflation stays high.
news_drafts.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Annex 1 - Medium Term Financial Plan 2027.28 - 2030.31

findings.headline: Additional Learning Needs represents 50% of school budget pressures, driven by rising demand and complexity of placements
findings.detail: The report identifies that "Current estimates suggest that 50% of schools pressure is in respect to ALN through a combination of funding for Special Schools places and Special Resource Base places within Local Authority maintained schools." The budget gap includes demand pressures for "Additional Learning Needs, and its associated impacts due to the rise in complexity, cost and number of placements needed at a time when supply is constrained. This includes in relation to Home to School Transport and education placements in out of LA maintained settings."
findings.matters: ALN demand is driving half of the school budget gap and represents a supply-constrained, cost-inflation-sensitive area where the council has limited control over volumes.
findings.figures: 50% of school pressures attributable to ALN
findings.quote: Current estimates suggest that 50% of schools pressure is in respect to ALN through a combination of funding for Special Schools places and Special Resource Base places within Local Authority maintained settings.

findings.headline: Useable reserves are comparably low for an authority of this size, limiting financial flexibility
findings.detail: The report's Financial Resilience Snapshot notes: "Whilst earmarked reserves have increased, informal benchmarking shows that Cardiff's useable reserves are comparably low for an authority of this size." The council has a £4 million Financial Resilience Mechanism budget, which "provides capacity to cope with an adverse fluctuation of just over 0.5 percentage points on current funding assumptions." Over the medium term, the council has limited buffer capacity.
findings.matters: A lender assessing resilience to shocks needs to know the council has low unallocated reserves relative to its size, limiting its ability to absorb unforeseen pressures.
findings.figures: £4 million Financial Resilience Mechanism budget; provides buffer for just 0.5% fluctuation on funding
findings.quote: informal benchmarking shows that Cardiff's useable reserves are comparably low for an authority of this size.

findings.headline: Post-16 Additional Learning Needs funding is scheduled to transfer from Welsh Government to councils in April 2028, but the adequacy of funding is unconfirmed
findings.detail: The council has been funding post-16 ALN provision through interim arrangements since September 2023. Technical guidance from Welsh Government in June 2026 indicates these interim arrangements will continue until April 2028, when responsibility and funding will be fully transferred to Local Authorities. The report states: "It will be key that full funding is transferred for this responsibility and so the position will be closely monitored." This represents a known future liability with uncertain funding.
findings.matters: A material cost is scheduled to transfer to the council's base budget in 18 months with no guarantee of adequate funding, creating a forward liability.
findings.figures: Transfer date: April 2028; interim arrangements in place since September 2023
findings.quote: Technical guidance issued by WG in June 2026 indicates that the interim arrangements will continue until April 2028, when the funding will be fully transferred to Local Authorities. It will be key that full funding is transferred for this responsibility and so the position will be closely monitored.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account is running a deficit of £1.6 million in 2027/28 and £10.6 million over the medium term, requiring use of HRA reserves
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget and MTFP indicated a temporary budget gap for the HRA, estimated at £1.576 million for 2027/28 and £10.62 million over the MTFP period, after assuming targeted efficiency savings of £4.16 million. The report states: "The budget gap will require use of the available HRA earmarked reserves in the medium term, but the position will need to be updated as to any potential additional efficiencies and mitigation available to the HRA. Whilst the longer-term replenishment of HRA reserves is predicted, non-achievement of efficiency savings and service change targets will further impact this position."
findings.matters: The council's housing company is running deficits and relying on reserve drawdowns. If efficiency savings are under-delivered, reserves will deplete faster, creating a resilience risk.
findings.figures: £1.576 million HRA deficit 2027/28; £10.62 million over MTFP; £4.16 million efficiency savings assumed
findings.quote: The budget gap will require use of the available HRA earmarked reserves in the medium term, but the position will need to be updated as to any potential additional efficiencies and mitigation available to the HRA.

findings.headline: Savings achievement rate declining: only 85% of 2025/26 savings targets were met, yet the council needs to deliver £119 million in savings across the medium term
findings.detail: The council achieved 85% of savings in 2025/26 (85% in 2024/25 was 79%; in earlier years 84% in 2023/24 and 92% in 2022/23). Against this trend, the council now needs to identify £119 million in savings across the medium-term plan, including £34.6 million in 2027/28 alone. The report acknowledges: "Given the scale of savings required is almost £119 million across the medium term, and over £34 million for 2027/28 alone, it will be necessary go beyond the traditional approach to identifying operational efficiencies."
findings.matters: A lender assessing financial resilience must factor in that historical savings delivery is below 90%, and the scale required (£119 million) is unprecedented, raising the risk of under-delivery and further deficits.
findings.figures: 85% savings achievement 2025/26; £34.615 million savings required 2027/28; £118.925 million savings required over MTFP
findings.quote: The percentage of savings achieved was 85% for 2025/26 (this is slightly higher than 2024/25 which was 79%, but lower than earlier years – with 84% achievement in 2023/24 and 92% in 2022/23.)
